At $x=50$, $4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\times 50\right)=4$.

The period of the sine function is $\dfrac{2\pi}{n}=8$, where $n=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

From $x=8$ to $x=48$, there are 5 complete cycles where the sine function is intersected twice.

Using the log laws first:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\Big[\ln\left(e^x\sin x\right)\Big]&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big[\ln e^x+\ln(\sin x)\Big]\\ &=\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big[x+\ln(\sin x)\Big]\\ &=1+\cot x \end{aligned}$$

Alternative, using the product rule:

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^x\sin x\right)=e^x\cos x+e^x\sin x$$

$$\begin{aligned} \therefore \dfrac{d}{dx}\Big[\ln\left(e^x\sin x\right)\Big]&=\dfrac{e^x(\cos x+\sin x)}{e^x\sin x}\\ &=\dfrac{\cos x+\sin x}{\sin x}\\ &=1+\cot x \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Let the sum of the original geometric series be $S_1$ and the new series (the cubes, first term $a^3$, ratio $r^3$) be $S_2$.

$$S_1=\dfrac{a}{1-r}=3\text{, so }a=3(1-r)\qquad(1)$$

$$S_2=\dfrac{a^3}{1-r^3}=\dfrac{27}{19}\qquad(2)$$

Substitute (1) into (2) and divide both sides by 27:

$$\dfrac{\big(3(1-r)\big)^3}{1-r^3}=\dfrac{27}{19}$$

$$\dfrac{(1-r)^3}{(1-r)(1+r+r^2)}=\dfrac{1}{19}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1-2r+r^2}{1+r+r^2}&=\dfrac{1}{19}\\ 6r^2-13r+6&=0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore r=\dfrac{3}{2}\text{ or }\dfrac{2}{3}$$

Since $|r|<1$ for a limiting sum:

$$\therefore r=\dfrac{2}{3}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: Correct answer; 2: Obtains $6r^2-13r+6=0$, or equivalent merit; 1: Writes $\dfrac{a^3}{1-r^3}=\dfrac{27}{19}$ for the series of cubes, or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{\sin x-\sin^3 x}\,dx&=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{\sin x\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)}\,dx\\ &=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{\sin x\cos^2 x}\,dx \end{aligned}$$

Since $x\in\left[0,\,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, $\cos x\ge 0$, so $\sqrt{\cos^2 x}=\cos x$.

$$\begin{aligned} &=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\cos x(\sin x)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\\ &=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{3}{2}\cos x(\sin x)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}\Big[(\sin x)^{\frac{3}{2}}\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}\left[\left(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}-(\sin 0)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]\\ &=\dfrac{2}{3}(1-0)\\ &=\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: Correct answer; 2: Correct primitive $\dfrac{2}{3}(\sin x)^{\frac{3}{2}}$, or equivalent merit; 1: Simplifies the integrand to $\cos x(\sin x)^{\frac{1}{2}}$, or equivalent merit

Method 1 (integrating with respect to $y$):

Since $y=20-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2$, $x=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{100-5y}}{2}$.

$$\begin{aligned} A&=2\int_0^{10}\dfrac{\sqrt{100-5y}}{2}\,dy\\ &=\int_0^{10}\sqrt{100-5y}\,dy\\ &=\left[-\dfrac{2}{15}(100-5y)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_0^{10}\\ &=-\dfrac{2}{15}\left(50^{\frac{3}{2}}-100^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{400}{3}-\dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$

The volume of the prism is the cross-sectional area times the width:

$$\begin{aligned} V&=Ah\\ &=\left(\dfrac{400}{3}-\dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)\times 4\\ &=\dfrac{1600-400\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^3 \end{aligned}$$

Method 2 (rectangle plus side regions): let $y=20-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2=10$, so $x=\pm\dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}$.

$$\begin{aligned} A&=2\times\dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}\times 10+2\int_{\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}^{5}\left(20-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2\right)dx\\ &=50\sqrt{2}+2\left[20x-\dfrac{4}{15}x^3\right]_{\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}^{5}\\ &=50\sqrt{2}+2\left(100-\dfrac{100}{3}-\left(50\sqrt{2}-\dfrac{25}{3}\sqrt{2}\right)\right)\\ &=50\sqrt{2}+2\left(\dfrac{200}{3}-\dfrac{125\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{400}{3}-\dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$

Method 3 (whole parabola minus the unshaded cap):

$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_{-5}^{5}\left(20-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2\right)dx-\int_{-\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}^{\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}\left(20-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2-10\right)dx\\ &=\left[20x-\dfrac{4}{15}x^3\right]_{-5}^{5}-\left[10x-\dfrac{4}{15}x^3\right]_{-\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}^{\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}}\\ &=\left(200-\dfrac{200}{3}\right)-\left(50\sqrt{2}-\dfrac{50\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{400}{3}-\dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$

In each method $V=4A=\dfrac{1600-400\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ cm}^3$.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 4: Correct proof; 3: Correct cross-sectional area $\dfrac{400}{3}-\dfrac{100\sqrt{2}}{3}$, or equivalent merit; 2: Correct integral expression for the cross-sectional area of the shampoo, or equivalent merit; 1: Finds $x=\pm\dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}$ at $y=10$, or $x$ in terms of $y$, or equivalent merit

Method 1: $y=\dfrac{4}{5}x^2$, so $x=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{5y}}{2}$.

$$\begin{aligned} A&=2\int_0^h\dfrac{\sqrt{5y}}{2}\,dy\\ &=\sqrt{5}\int_0^h\sqrt{y}\,dy\\ &=\sqrt{5}\times\dfrac{2}{3}\Big[y^{\frac{3}{2}}\Big]_0^h\\ &=\dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}\left(h^{\frac{3}{2}}-0\right)\\ &=\dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}h^{\frac{3}{2}} \end{aligned}$$

Method 2: $h=\dfrac{4}{5}x^2$ gives $x=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{5h}}{2}$.

$$\begin{aligned} A&=2\int_0^{\frac{\sqrt{5h}}{2}}\left(h-\dfrac{4}{5}x^2\right)dx\\ &=2\left[hx-\dfrac{4}{15}x^3\right]_0^{\frac{\sqrt{5h}}{2}}\\ &=2\left(h\times\dfrac{\sqrt{5h}}{2}-\dfrac{4}{15}\times\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{5h}}{2}\right)^3-(0-0)\right)\\ &=\sqrt{5}h^{\frac{3}{2}}-\dfrac{\sqrt{5}h^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}h^{\frac{3}{2}} \end{aligned}$$

The area of the uniform cross-section of shampoo remains the same, so using part (a):

$$\dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}h^{\frac{3}{2}}=\dfrac{400-100\sqrt{2}}{3}$$

$$h^{\frac{3}{2}}=\dfrac{400-100\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{5}}=40\sqrt{5}-10\sqrt{10}$$

$$\therefore h=\left(40\sqrt{5}-10\sqrt{10}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}\text{ cm}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 4: Correct proof; 3: Equates the cross-sectional area to $\dfrac{400-100\sqrt{2}}{3}$, or equivalent merit; 2: Finds the cross-sectional area $\dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}h^{\frac{3}{2}}$, or equivalent merit; 1: Correct integral expression for the area in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit

The account balance at the end of the first 6 years can be determined using the future value table at 2.50% for 6 periods, multiplied by the deposit amount of \$15 000:

$$6.38774\times\$15\,000=\$95\,816.10$$

This amount will continue to accrue interest for the remaining 9 years at 2.50% per annum, so we multiply it by $1.025^9$.

Similarly, the four \$20 000 deposits (end of years 7 to 10) are worth $4.15252\times\$20\,000$ at the end of year 10, and accrue interest for 5 more years:

$$4.15252\times\$20\,000\times 1.025^5$$

Thus, the final account balance at the end of 15 years is:

$$6.38774\times\$15\,000\times 1.025^9+4.15252\times\$20\,000\times 1.025^5=\$213\,625.08\text{ (nearest cent)}$$

Alternate method (in stages, rounding to the nearest cent):

At the end of 6 years: $6.38774\times\$15\,000=\$95\,816.10$

At the end of 10 years: $4.15252\times\$20\,000+\$95\,816.10\times 1.025^4=\$188\,813.45$

At the end of 15 years: $\$188\,813.45\times 1.025^5=\$213\,625.09$

Depending on how granularly the stages are considered, the final result will differ by a few cents due to rounding.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 4: Correct answer with sufficient reasoning; 3: Applies the interest rate in the years after deposits have stopped, or equivalent merit; 2: Takes the appropriate products of deposit amount and future value, or equivalent merit; 1: Identifies the appropriate values in the table

The shaded area is the integral of the difference between the curves between their points of intersection; $y=xe^{-x}$ is the upper curve.

To find the points of intersection, equate the two expressions for $y$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x}{e}&=xe^{-x}\\ xe^{-1}&=xe^{-x} \end{aligned}$$

So $x=0$ or $e^{-1}=e^{-x}$, giving $x=1$.

Hence, the shaded area is:

$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 xe^{-x}-\dfrac{x}{e}\,dx&=\left[-e^{-x}-xe^{-x}-\dfrac{x^2}{2e}\right]_0^1\\ &=\left(-e^{-1}-e^{-1}-\dfrac{1}{2e}\right)-(-1-0-0)\\ &=1-\dfrac{5}{2e} \end{aligned}$$

The median, $m$, is given by $F(m)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, where $0\le m\le 2$.

Method 1:

$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left(5-m^2\right)+1&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left(5-m^2\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \ln\left(5-m^2\right)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 5=\ln\sqrt{5}\\ 5-m^2&=\sqrt{5}\\ m^2&=5-\sqrt{5} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore m=\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}\quad(\text{since }0\le m\le 2)$$

Method 2:

$$\begin{aligned} p\left(\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left[5-\left(\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}\right)^2\right]+1\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\left[5-\left(5-\sqrt{5}\right)\right]+1\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}\ln\sqrt{5}+1\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}+1\quad\left[\ln\sqrt{5}=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 5\right]\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: Correct proof; 1: Sets $F(m)=\dfrac{1}{2}$ using the expression from part (b), or equivalent merit

$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\dfrac{1}{16}x^2\left(5-2\sqrt{x}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{16}\left(5x^2-2x^{2.5}\right) \end{aligned}$$

The pdf is $F'(x)$:

$$\begin{aligned} F'(x)&=\dfrac{1}{16}\left(10x-5x^{1.5}\right)\\ F''(x)&=\dfrac{1}{16}\left(10-7.5x^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)\\ F'''(x)&=\dfrac{1}{32}\left(-7.5x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) \end{aligned}$$

The mode is where the pdf takes its greatest value in $0\le x\le 4$.

$$\begin{aligned} F''(x)=0\text{, so }\dfrac{1}{16}\left(10-7.5x^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)&=0\\ 7.5x^{\frac{1}{2}}&=10\\ x^{\frac{1}{2}}&=\dfrac{10}{7.5}=\dfrac{4}{3}\\ x&=\dfrac{16}{9} \end{aligned}$$

$F'''\left(\dfrac{16}{9}\right)<0$, so the pdf has a global maximum there.

$$\therefore \text{mode}=\dfrac{16}{9}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: Correct answer; 2: Solves $F''(x)=0$ for $x$, or equivalent merit; 1: Finds the pdf $F'(x)$, or equivalent merit

Let $n=2022$. Using part (a):

$$2022\times 2023\times 2024\times 2025+1=\left(n^2+3n\right)\left(n^2+3n+2\right)+1$$

Let $k=n^2+3n$ (an integer).

$$\begin{aligned} 2022\times 2023\times 2024\times 2025+1&=k(k+2)+1\\ &=k^2+2k+1\\ &=(k+1)^2 \end{aligned}$$

where $k+1$ is an integer.

$\therefore 2022\times 2023\times 2024\times 2025+1$ is a perfect square.

Alternate method: let $n=2022$ and $k=n^2+3n+1$. Then

$$\begin{aligned} 2022\times 2023\times 2024\times 2025+1&=(k-1)(k+1)+1=k^2\\ &=\left(n^2+3n+1\right)^2 \end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: Correct deduction; 1: Writes the expression as $\left(n^2+3n\right)\left(n^2+3n+2\right)+1$ with $n=2022$, or equivalent merit
